										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>UCLA</strong> published a technical paper titled “Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for chip design, but most existing approaches operate directly at RTL. We ask whether agents can design better chips by leveraging higher-level abstractions. We compare Direct RTL Design, Agent-based HLS Design, Post-Compiler HLS Refinement, and Post-HLS RTL Refinement, and combine Agent-based HLS Design with Post-HLS RTL Refinement as Agent-based HLS with RTL Refinement (AHRR).”</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21157">Find the technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p>Ding, Zijian, Yang Zou, Yizhou Sun, and Jason Cong. “Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?” arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.21157 (September 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21157</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

		<title>How 60 GHz Radar Improves Low-Power Presence Sensing In IoT Devices</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-60-ghz-radar-improves-low-power-presence-sensing-in-iot-devices/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-60-ghz-radar-improves-low-power-presence-sensing-in-iot-devices/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Chris Wengerter]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 21 Sep 2026 07:01:47 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Secured Intelligent Mobility]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[antenna in package]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[FMCW radar]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Infineon]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[low power]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[MCU]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[presence sensing]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[sensors]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281654</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Track occupancy and motion continuously without keeping the full sensing and processing chain active.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-60-ghz-radar-improves-low-power-presence-sensing-in-iot-devices/">How 60 GHz Radar Improves Low-Power Presence Sensing In IoT Devices</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Battery-powered IoT devices must maintain room-level awareness without keeping their full sensing and processing chains continuously active. A duty-cycled architecture built around sensors that detect larger body motion and micro-motion allows smart thermostats, occupancy sensors, and security systems to monitor occupancy, track motion, and wake downstream hardware only when needed.</p>
<p>This article reviews how 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar supports low-power presence sensing in IoT designs. It uses Infineon’s <a href="https://www.infineon.com/part/BGT60CUTR13AIP">XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP</a> as an implementation example of antenna-in-package (AIP) integration, on-chip radar processing, and autonomous low-power operation for occupancy and motion detection without continuous host-side processing.</p>
<h2>Sensor limitations in low-power presence detection</h2>
<p>Passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect changes in infrared radiation as a person moves relative to the sensor. Low power draw and low cost explain their widespread use in occupancy devices, yet PIR output is limited to simple binary motion events with no range, angle, or fine-movement data. Dependence on thermal contrast also creates false-trigger risk and causes missed occupancy when people remain stationary. PIR sensors also require a clear field of view through an infrared-transparent window or lens, which constrains sensor placement and enclosure design.</p>
<p>In applications such as video doorbells and security cameras, the camera performs the product’s primary imaging function. After a low-power sensor triggers system wake-up, the camera provides visual verification and richer scene context. However, using the camera for continuous presence detection keeps the image sensor, host processor, memory, and image-processing pipeline active and increases average current in battery-powered products. Cameras also require optical windows, clear fields of view, and adequate illumination. These requirements limit mechanical design flexibility.</p>
<p>Ultrasonic sensing provides a non-optical option for proximity detection, though acoustic noise, airflow, temperature variation, and material reflections degrade sensor performance. Spatial detail is also limited, reducing the sensor’s ability to detect fine motion or separate occupants and objects by range.</p>
<p>These constraints shift low-power presence sensing from component selection to system architecture. Designers need an always-available sensing front end that detects occupancy and motion without keeping higher-power sensing, processing, or imaging blocks active.</p>
<h2>FMCW radar as an active sensing method</h2>
<p>A 60 GHz-band frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar provides the required front end for accurate, low-power presence sensing by using RF measurement instead of thermal contrast, optical imaging, or acoustic propagation. The transmitter emits a continuous waveform whose frequency sweeps over time. Reflections from people and objects return to the receiver, where differences between transmitted and received signals provide range and motion information.</p>
<p>For compact IoT devices, 60 GHz operation reduces antenna dimensions, while wide FMCW bandwidth provides fine range resolution for short-range indoor sensing. FMCW sensing also supports occupancy detection after larger body motion stops, as breathing, posture shifts, and other micro-motion create measurable changes in the returned signal. These signal changes allow radar to detect presence when motion-only sensors no longer register movement.</p>
<p>RF sensing further reduces dependence on environmental conditions that affect PIR, camera, and ultrasonic sensors. Operation in darkness, bright sunlight, smoke, or steam, along with placement behind RF-transparent or low-loss enclosure materials, gives designers more flexibility in enclosure design and sensor placement.</p>
<p>Infineon’s XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP implements this sensing model as a 57 to 64 GHz CMOS radar sensor with 7 GHz FMCW bandwidth. With a detection range of approximately 0.025 m to 20 m, the sensor covers close interaction sensing and room-scale occupancy detection.<strong><br />
</strong></p>
<h2>Integrated radar architecture for compact IoT designs</h2>
<p>The BGT60CUTR13AIP combines the radar monolithic microwave integrated circuit (MMIC), antenna structures, internal low-dropout regulators, an oscillator, and control logic in a compact antenna-in-package device measuring approximately 6.05 mm × 4.3 mm × 0.9 mm.</p>
<p>Moving the antennas and support circuitry into the package reduces external RF structures, controlled RF routing, antenna placement, and board-level tuning required in discrete radar designs. Integration also minimizes external component count, simplifies the bill of materials (BOM), limits always-connected components that add standby current, and improves design repeatability in space-constrained IoT products.</p>
<p>The AIP design integrates one transmit antenna and three receive antennas in an L-shaped array for azimuth and elevation sensing. This layout provides a field of view up to 150 degrees in both azimuth and elevation, enabling room-scale presence sensing from wall-mounted, ceiling-mounted, or embedded product locations.</p>
<h2>On-chip processing and host-MCU wake-up</h2>
<p>On-chip processing extends integration from the RF front end to signal analysis. By shifting radar processing from the host MCU to the sensor, the BGT60CUTR13AIP reduces continuous host-side processing of the radar data stream.</p>
<p>An integrated hardware accelerator handles computationally demanding radar functions, including 2D fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), filtering, constant false alarm rate (CFAR) processing, and angle-of-arrival estimation. A moving-target indication (MTI) function supports autonomous motion detection. When the radar identifies relevant activity, an interrupt wakes the host MCU to execute higher-level application logic.</p>
<p>Partitioning keeps environmental monitoring on the radar front end while reserving the host system for application logic, wireless communication, display control, camera activation, or cloud interaction. Host-level processing occurs only when a radar-detected event warrants a system response.</p>
<h2>System power benefits of radar-triggered operation</h2>
<p>An event-triggered model reduces average current by limiting how long higher-power subsystems remain active between events. Keeping the MCU, camera, display, or radio awake increases power consumption even when each component has efficient active-mode specifications.</p>
<p>Low-power radar changes the system duty-cycle profile by keeping an always-available sensing front end active while higher-power subsystems remain off or in low-power standby. The BGT60CUTR13AIP supports sensing modes below 1 mW and deep-sleep operation around 0.1 mW, allowing activity monitoring without full-system operation.</p>
<p>In a security-camera architecture, radar functions as a first-stage trigger. The sensor monitors for presence or movement in a defined region, then activates image capture only when the event requires imaging. This reduces unnecessary processing, heat generation, and data capture during idle periods.</p>
<p>Radar-triggered operation also extends to displays, thermostats, occupancy sensors, and lighting controls, allowing these systems to respond to presence or proximity without continuous host-side processing.</p>
<h2>Applications in smart home and building systems</h2>
<p>Radar-based presence sensing enables smart home and building devices that require more detailed occupancy context than a binary motion event. In lighting and HVAC systems, micro-motion detection helps prevent false vacancy decisions when occupants remain still and allows control algorithms to differentiate empty rooms from quietly occupied spaces.</p>
<p>In consumer electronics, radar supports proximity-aware operation without optical capture. Smart TVs, monitors, speakers, and displays use proximity data to respond as people enter a room, approach the device, or leave the space while avoiding continuous image sensing.</p>
<p>Security applications use radar as a presence-aware front end for imaging, transmission, or recording functions, activating higher-power subsystems only after motion or presence is detected in a defined region.</p>
<p>More advanced implementations, such as room activity classification, gesture-based controls, and vital-sign monitoring, extend radar sensing beyond occupancy detection. Each use case requires application-specific firmware, placement, and validation, yet the sensing architecture remains consistent: low-power radar delivers local perception without continuous image capture or host-side processing.</p>
<h2>Development and integration considerations</h2>
<p>Adding RF sensing to compact IoT products introduces antenna, layout, regulatory, and test requirements. Infineon supports these requirements through the BGT60CUTR13AIP’s antenna-in-package design, FCC-certified reference designs, and developer resources. The integrated antenna structure reduces RF layout complexity while giving teams a validated starting point for product development.</p>
<p>Mechanical integration of presence-sensing devices benefits from radar placement behind RF-transparent or low-loss enclosure materials. Unlike cameras and PIR sensors, radar does not require a lens, optical window, or visible aperture, supporting sealed housings and discreet placement in residential and workplace environments.</p>
<p>Beyond mechanical design, Infineon provides <a href="https://softwaretools.infineon.com/tools/com.ifx.tb.tool.modustoolbox">ModusToolbox software tools</a>, evaluation kits, and documentation for IoT use cases. These resources support prototyping, validation, and firmware partitioning between the radar sensor and host MCU while helping teams coordinate RF design, enclosure integration, and application development.</p>
<h2>Conclusion</h2>
<p>Reliable IoT presence detection requires a sensing front end that tracks occupancy and motion continuously without keeping the full sensing and processing chain active. PIR, camera, and ultrasonic sensors impose tradeoffs in spatial coverage, power draw, optical access, and environmental sensitivity that limit their use as always-on solutions in battery-powered designs.</p>
<p>Infineon’s XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP 60 GHz CMOS radar sensor combines FMCW sensing, 7 GHz bandwidth, antenna-in-package integration, on-chip acceleration, and autonomous host-MCU wake-up to support local occupancy awareness without continuous full-system operation. For smart home, smart building, security, display, and battery-powered sensing designs, this 60 GHz radar architecture provides a compact front end for more reliable presence detection within constrained power and space budgets.</p>
<p>— Rewritten by Chris Wengerter, based on original text written and published by Wevolver in April 2026.</p>

		<title>How Robotics And Intelligent Equipment Control Drive Next-Gen Fab Productivity</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-robotics-and-intelligent-equipment-control-drive-next-gen-fab-productivity/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-robotics-and-intelligent-equipment-control-drive-next-gen-fab-productivity/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Laura Peters]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 21 Sep 2026 07:01:36 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[acoustic inspection]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[Lam Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Microtronic]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PDF Solutions]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[preventive maintenance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[robotics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[thermal inspection]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[tool fingerprinting]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Behind the scenes, advanced equipment control and robotics are enabling higher levels of repeatability, tool uptime, and yield. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-robotics-and-intelligent-equipment-control-drive-next-gen-fab-productivity/">How Robotics And Intelligent Equipment Control Drive Next-Gen Fab Productivity</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Autonomous inspection robots detect overheating, leaks, and equipment anomalies in fabs before they cause failures, while keeping technicians out of hazardous environments.</li>
<li>Connecting equipment conditions, material data, and wafer results helps engineers identify process variation, improve chamber matching, and maintain tighter process control.</li>
<li>Collaborative robots automate chamber cleaning and other maintenance tasks, reducing human error and accelerating equipment recovery. Fully autonomous fabs, however, still face technical and infrastructure challenges.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Robotics and AI are taking on more tasks in fabs today, particularly to reduce unscheduled downtime and ensure more good wafers are produced with existing capacity.</p>
<p>Both leading and legacy fabs are boosting operational uptime using collaborative robots and autonomous vehicles equipped with sensors to replace many of the mundane tasks performed by humans in the past. Automation ensures repeatability, reserving human intervention for problem-solving activity.</p>
<p>At the same time, process engineers now have the computing capability at their fingertips to better tie together equipment state, process context, and wafer results, one of the pivotal ways they keep variation under control despite fabricating devices with nanometer-scale critical dimensions and tolerances.</p>
<p>“The strongest quality-control strategies connect material data, equipment data, and wafer results so that subtle sources of variation can be detected before they become a yield problem,” said Jon Holt, worldwide fab applications solutions manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/pdf-solutions/">PDF Solutions</a>. “A material may meet its incoming specification yet behave differently because of delivery-line condition, temperature history, residence time, chamber condition, or interaction with another material. Modern equipment-control and data-collection systems help preserve this context, enforce operating limits, identify drift, and prevent processing when critical parameters fall outside an approved range.”</p>
<p>Rising manufacturing costs, global expansion and labor shortages all contribute to greater implementation of automation, robotics and AI.</p>
<p>“There are three trends driving big advances in equipment intelligence,” said Russell Dover, managing director of equipment intelligence product development at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/lam-research/">Lam Research</a>. “One is the increasing cost of manufacturing and the critical need to get as much productivity and ROI from existing investments. When I started at a fab in the UK over 30 years ago, a fab cost around $20 million. Now that barely covers a set of equipment, with a gigascale fab costing around $20 billion. Second, fabs are booming in new geographic locations, so companies want to replicate the capabilities of a fab in one region in a similar fab in a completely different location, creating interesting fleet-management challenges. Third, our significant talent gap is fueling a need for more automation, AI, machine learning, and robotics — not to replace people, but to embrace robotics to consistently perform repetitive or tedious tasks while taking better advantage of human ingenuity and the speed advantages that ML and AI can afford.”</p>
<p><strong>Robots and cobots improve precision, ensure safety</strong><br />
Intel Foundry uses Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robot to provide real-time monitoring of equipment conditions, largely behind-the-scenes in the subfab (see figure 1). There, hot motors, pumps or electrical equipment may give off a thermal signature due to an impending overheating situation. Failing motors tend to vibrate. Leaking air or specialty gases can make high-frequency sounds that acoustic imaging systems can differentiate from background noise. Such robots also can perform routine, simple tasks that require weaving through tight spaces to record readings on digital or analog gauges. Intel Foundry’s outfitted robot, called Chip, play an important role in maintaining equipment health in multiple facilities without requiring a technician or engineer to physically visit a location just to record and report back routine readings to a host controller.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24281649" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.25-PM.png?resize=550%2C448&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="550" height="448" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.25-PM.png?w=724&amp;ssl=1 724w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.25-PM.png?resize=300%2C244&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.25-PM.png?resize=600%2C489&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 550px) 100vw, 550px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 1: Intel Foundry equips the Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robot to continually perform visual, thermal, and acoustic inspections in its subfabs, ultrapure water, and air cooling/distribution facilities. Photo: Semiconductor Engineering</strong></p>
<p>So far, Intel says its robots can perform 16 different preventive inspection tasks using visual, thermal, and acoustic inspections, in addition to lidar and RealSense depth cameras. This approach improves the quality of data collected during inspections by streamlining the process for technicians and decreasing safety risks.</p>
<p>“For example, during a routine inspection of boiler pumps, Chip detected hot water unexpectedly moving through the line of a powered-down pump,” explained Joe Robinson, IoT &amp; Robotics Architect at Intel Foundry in a recent article. [1] “The robot alerted area technicians about the anomaly, enabling them to safely isolate the pump for diagnosis. Technicians found a non-functioning gasket in the pump. Together, this proactive repair by humans and a robot prevented possible hot water leakage and additional equipment damage.”</p>
<p>In practical fab terms, Intel Foundry is using Chip robots to perform:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Thermal inspection:</strong> Finding hot motors, pumps, electrical components, and other equipment before overheating becomes a failure.</li>
<li><strong>Acoustic inspection:</strong> Detecting abnormal sounds and potentially air/gas leaks or mechanical problems that have an acoustic signature.</li>
<li><strong>Visual inspection:</strong> Cameras and AI can repeatedly examine equipment, gauges, and other inspection points rather than relying solely on technician recordings.</li>
<li><strong>Trend/predictive maintenance:</strong> Repeated robotic inspections create time-series data that Intel can analyze to detect equipment drift toward failure and schedule maintenance before an unscheduled shutdown<strong>. </strong></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Safety drives new automation solutions</strong><br />
Robotics and automation are especially important after emergencies. For example, fab personnel in earthquake-prone Taiwan have found a better way to recover from a disaster. Robots now perform safety inspections, which would otherwise expose personnel to gas leaks, toxic chemicals, or collapsing objects.</p>
<p>UMC&#8217;s fab facility, smart manufacturing and IT teams together developed an Autonomous Mobile inspection Robot (AMR) to safely replace manual inspections. Formerly, each day two technicians would spend 1 hour or more to complete routine inspections, which are now performed automatically.</p>
<p>In a similar manner to Intel’s approach, UMC’s AMR uses ultrasonic acoustic cameras to detect high-frequency sound waves to pinpoint gas or liquid leaks or detect sound wave oscillations caused by vibrating equipment. The robot’s AI precisely locates potential sources of anomalies and triggers early intervention by the preventive maintenance team to address equipment problems and prevent equipment damage.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281650" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=1996%2C1218&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1996" height="1218" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?w=1996&amp;ssl=1 1996w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=300%2C183&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=1024%2C625&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=768%2C469&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=1536%2C937&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.51.54-PM.png?resize=600%2C366&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: The Autonomous Mobile Inspection Robot (AMR) helps preventive maintenance teams identify thermal signatures, gas leaks, liquid puddles, and records readings on gauges. Source: UMC</strong></p>
<p>The AMRs also use thermal sensors to detect hidden signs of equipment overheating as well as liquid leakage, common hazards in fabs and subfabs. The thermal imaging system can detect liquid residues on the ground that are difficult to see with the naked eye, identify leaks in a timely manner, and clearly indicate potentially overheating parts so engineering personnel can quickly address problem areas.</p>
<p><strong>How equipment control reduces wafer variation</strong><br />
Process variation is becoming increasingly critical with every new device node. “As device dimensions continue to shrink and process windows tighten, nearly every process becomes more sensitive to variation, but patterning, deposition, etch, CMP, and thermal processes are especially critical,” said Alan Weber, vice president of new product innovations at PDF Solutions. “Small differences in chamber conditions, material delivery, temperature, pressure, plasma behavior, endpoint detection, or equipment state can translate into meaningful changes in critical dimensions, film properties, overlay, uniformity, and ultimately device performance and yield.”</p>
<p>Engineers are going after multiple sources of variation. “Advanced device architectures require more selective processes, thinner and more conformal films, and tighter control of interfaces between materials. This makes the condition and history of the equipment increasingly important,” said Patrick Pannese, vice president of strategy and business development at PDF Solutions. “Variation may arise not only between tools, but also between chambers, recipes, maintenance cycles, consumable lifetimes, and even successive wafers within the same lot. Consequently, equipment health monitoring, high-frequency data collection, chamber matching, run-to-run control, and correlation of equipment data with wafer results are becoming essential parts of process control.”</p>
<p><strong>Returning process tools to useful production status faster</strong><br />
Generally, whether it is at the process tool or subfab equipment level, fabs are increasingly interested in moving from unscheduled downtime to predictive maintenance. “Any time you can use machine learning and analytics to predict that something is failing, you can move from what would become an unscheduled event into a scheduled event that is also very attractive from a fab operational standpoint,” said Lam Research’s Dover.</p>
<p>For example, Lam Research offers both plasma-based etching equipment and deposition equipment that requires a repeatable chamber condition before process wafer runs. “We use the optical emission spectroscopy (OES) data from a plasma to indicate when a chamber is ready to process wafers. For instance, right after a chamber has been cleaned during maintenance, it is not prepared to run wafers,” said Dover. “First, it needs to be ‘conditioned,’ or uniformly coated with a film. Most conditioning is based on a learned limit, running the plasma in the tool for 25, 50, 100, or 200 RF hours while running dummy wafers until the surfaces are uniformly coated. This does give you a known condition, and it works.”</p>
<p>“But if you look at the OES spectrum, you can start to determine when you actually achieve that condition,&#8221; he said. &#8220;This is important for two reasons. One, you get that chamber back into production sooner, so we improve the tool availability and get more wafers out. The second is that the life of a chamber between maintenance cycles is a function of the total RF hours. If you&#8217;re burning 200 to 300 hours just doing seasoning, that&#8217;s 200 to 300 hours that gets subtracted from useful production because it goes toward the next maintenance cycle.”</p>
<p><strong>Tool-to-tool matching</strong><br />
Within a given fab, process engineers routinely perform tool-to-tool matching to ensure wafers processed by different tools using the same materials and the same recipe produce the same results. “The primary goal of tool matching (and its first cousin, chamber matching) is to avoid the dedication of specific production equipment and its subsystems to certain critical products or layers just because they come out better on these &#8216;golden tools,'&#8221; explained Steve Zamek, director of product management at PDF Solutions. “This approach not only complicates factory scheduling, but also reduces overall capacity of the fab.&#8221;</p>
<p>Both are undesirable side effects. &#8220;Run-to-run technology can be applied to capture the current tool state so that this can be factored into subsequent runs using feedforward models that combine material state and tool state to then adjust recipe parameters to achieve the desired result,&#8221; Zamek said. &#8220;A more robust approach uses so-called fingerprinting technology to characterize the underlying mechanisms in the equipment that can affect the process result (power generation, flow control, pressure control, etc.) and ensure that these mechanisms in all tools that need to be in a “matched set” are brought within tight tolerance of the reference tool or specification. The assumption underlying this approach is that if all individual components of the equipment are behaving consistently (i.e., they are &#8216;matched&#8217;), then the tool in aggregate should behave consistently, as well.”</p>
<p>With global expansion of fab activity, which is forecast to double the size of the semiconductor industry within five years, there is pent-up need to apply “matching” procedures from one fab to another, taking quality control to even higher levels.</p>
<p>Many process tools, such as deposition, etching, and annealing systems, contain multiple identical chambers under vacuum to accelerate throughput. For these systems, chamber-to-chamber matching is important because a problem on every third wafer or every fifth wafer in a lot can be missed, impacting yield down the line. A macro defect inspection tool equipped with randomization features can detect subtle differences between wafers using randomization to provide insight about where process variation originated.</p>
<p>“In one example, a slight difference in signal intensity showed a difference in topography of only about 1,000 angstroms of BPSG (boron phosphosilicate glass), but it occurred only on one out of every third wafer,” said Errol Akomer, applications director at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/microtronic/">Microtronic</a>. “Using a randomization strategy where wafer position is shuffled within lots, problems that occur on particular wafers can be traced back to their source more quickly.” [3]</p>
<p><strong>Here come the cobots</strong><br />
The semiconductor industry has been using x-axis robots for wafer handling inside process tools, die inside pick-and-place tools, as well as automation for moving wafer lots (FOUPs) between tools in the fab for decades. What’s different about cobots is that they are not fully tied to one piece of equipment and can be reconfigured to manage new situations. For instance, the same cobot can remove screws from a chamber opening and perform chamber cleaning using different end effectors and recipes (see figure 2).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281651" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=1670%2C704&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1670" height="704" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?w=1670&amp;ssl=1 1670w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=300%2C126&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=1024%2C432&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=768%2C324&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=1536%2C648&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-18-at-3.52.11-PM.png?resize=600%2C253&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 3: The collaborative robot (cobot) performs maintenance procedures using different end effectors to loosen screws and clean the chamber in a safer, more repeatable manner than a human can. Source: Lam Research </strong></p>
<p>One of the key areas of focus for cobots is reducing unscheduled downtime. ‘Most unscheduled downtime comes from mistakes that happened during preventive maintenance,” said Lam Research’s Dover. “We recently introduced our Dextro cobot with multiple end effectors, which can clean process chambers using a dry ice spray, for instance, with a higher level of precision and repeatability than a human performing the same task, while ensuring a higher level of safety. For example, even when the cobot is driving in screws, a person has a hard time applying exactly the same amount of torque each time, but this is not an issue for a cobot. And semiconductor process tools are not designed ergonomically, so technicians have to adapt to the tool, not the other way around. There are also savings from the standpoint of PPE (personal protective equipment) and the time needed to bring in and train technicians.”</p>
<p>When applied across hundreds of tools, the result can be substantial bottom-line cost savings. “Our customers not only document better outcomes in terms of the preventive maintenance procedures being done correctly, but the reduction in variability is showing up as improved Cpk and marginal yield, which can amount to thousands to millions of dollars,” said Dover. The greater repeatability also improves tool-to-tool performance matching and equipment uptime.</p>
<p><strong>Dreams of the “lights out” fab</strong><br />
Ever since the development of the front-opening unified pod (FOUP), chipmakers have talked about the dream of fully autonomous fabs where on-site engineers and technicians are needed only to work behind the scenes. For some, this dream includes the use of humanoid robots.</p>
<p>“A number of key customers have visions of autonomous fabs or lights-out fabs, sort of a “Star Trek Next Generation” view with humanoid robots that just go around and do the work,” said Dover. “Whether that is pure science fiction, or whether the current leaps and bounds in AI technology will actually get us there, I don&#8217;t know. But I do know that people are aspiring to have humanoid robots doing preventive maintenance.&#8221;</p>
<p>It’s important to note that these robots have to interoperate with SEMI standards, host communication, and host control. “Compliance with SEMI standards would increase the building space by 30% versus non-SEMI compliance because you need safe paths for people, so the cost factor is way bigger than people are assuming,” said Dover. Also, there are other incompatibilities. “For instance, a humanoid robot operates for a limited time on a battery pack, and some of these maintenance routines take 12 hours. There are significant power issues to be overcome.”</p>
<p>So as humanoid robots mature, many fabs are reaping the benefits of inspection robots and cobots to help keep equipment in the fab, subfab, ultrapure water, and other supporting facilities up-and-running.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at <strong>Peking University</strong> published a technical paper titled “Predictive Structure to Thermal Conductivity Modeling Framework for BEOL Interconnect Stacks in Advanced Technology Nodes Enabled by Extensive Layer Resolved Thermal Measurements.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong> “The increasing structural complexity of BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced integrated circuits demands a structure-aware thermal conductivity (κ) modeling framework. However, generalizable models derived from layer-resolved thermal measurements that quantitatively capture the dependence of κ on interconnect structures remain lacking, limiting predictive thermal analysis. Here, we establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware κ modeling framework enabled by time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with ~100 nm depth resolution. Statistical analysis of a compiled dataset comprising over 40 experimentally measured layer-resolved κ values across diverse BEOL layers reveals a generalizable empirical structure-to-κ relationship, enabling predictive modeling based on interconnect structure. An intra-layer three-dimensional κ distribution model based on effective medium theory and realistic layouts further resolves spatial κ variations within practical interconnect layers. Together, these models establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware κ modeling framework for predictive and generalizable thermal analysis of advanced interconnect stacks and 3D ICs.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20379">Find the technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Huang, Zifeng, Yiyang Sun, Tianyu Jia, Runsheng Wang, and Zhe Cheng. “Predictive Structure to Thermal Conductivity Modeling Framework for BEOL Interconnect Stacks in Advanced Technology Nodes Enabled by Extensive Layer Resolved Thermal Measurements.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.20379 (September 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.20379</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at New York University published a technical paper titled “Routing Dense Layouts with History-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning using LSTM.” Abstract Excerpt: “Detailed routing remains a dominant runtime bottleneck in physical design due to increasing complexity of design rules. Modern routers can struggle to resolve persistent violations under dense operating conditions. While recent work leverages... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/reinforcement-learning-cuts-routing-violations-in-dense-chip-layouts-nyu/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/reinforcement-learning-cuts-routing-violations-in-dense-chip-layouts-nyu/">Reinforcement Learning Cuts Routing Violations in Dense Chip Layouts  (NYU)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>New York University</strong> published a technical paper titled “Routing Dense Layouts with History-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning using LSTM.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Detailed routing remains a dominant runtime bottleneck in physical design due to increasing complexity of design rules. Modern routers can struggle to resolve persistent violations under dense operating conditions. While recent work leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to dynamically select costs for each routing iteration, we find that this technique struggles with high-density designs where routing solutions are significantly harder. To address this, we present a history-aware offline RL policy which predicts iterative cost weights in these dense regimes to improve convergence across placement densities by utilizing readily available features from the router.&#8221;</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08232">Find the technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p>Khan, Afsara, and Austin Rovinski. “Routing Dense Layouts with History-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning using LSTM.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.08232 (September 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.08232</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/reinforcement-learning-cuts-routing-violations-in-dense-chip-layouts-nyu/">Reinforcement Learning Cuts Routing Violations in Dense Chip Layouts  (NYU)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the <strong>University of Edinburgh</strong> published a technical perspective titled “LLMs in Digital EDA: A perspective on shifting roles from Generation to Orchestration.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong> “In this Perspective, we instead define three hierarchical roles that reveal how capability accumulates: a Generator that produces design artifacts in a single pass, an Agent that refines outputs through iterative tool feedback, and an Orchestrator that coordinates decisions across EDA-stages. Across published systems, this reveals a syntax trap in which models are trained to produce plausible code rather than physically correct hardware, compounded by fragmented tools and loss of design context that obscure how decisions affect later stages. Comparisons across the three roles show that current approaches struggle to scale to industrial designs, motivating a shift towards a standardised, physics-aware orchestrator that connects tools and agents across the EDA flow for more reliable and accessible hardware design.”</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27184">Find the technical paper here</a>. August 2026.</p>
<p>Youngman, Matthew, Cristian Sestito, and Themis Prodromakis. “LLMs in Digital EDA: A perspective on shifting roles from Generation to Orchestration.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.27184 (August 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.27184</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Heidelberg University</strong> published a technical paper titled “A Unified Interconnection Network for Chiplet-Based Scaling of the BrainScaleS Neuromorphic System.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong> “To overcome the challenges of scaling analog designs, chiplet-based designs offer a promising approach with cost and flexibility advantages over monolithic scaling. Implementing a chiplet-based BSS-2* architecture requires an interconnection network that handles two distinct classes of traffic: error-tolerant traffic such as spikes and error-intolerant traffic like configuration data or data exchanged by the processing units. This work presents the design of a routing chiplet for the BSS-2 architecture that enables interconnection of multiple BSS-2 units in a 2D mesh topology. ”</p>
<p>*BrainScaleS-2 (BSS-2) neuromorphic architecture</p>
